KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

Strong high pressure remains in place tonight. It will be a 
tricky low temp forecast however as high cirrus outflow clouds 
from the remnants of Isaias are already spilling into the local 
area. I do not believe clouds will be thick enough to affect 
radiational cooling except for the southernmost counties in NH. 
I still think some upper 30s remain possible for those zones 
though, so no planned headline changes are anticipated. I did 
also add some patchy fog to the major river valleys, as warm 
waters should at least provide some steam fog if not radiation 
fog settling into the low lying areas. 

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

Then most of Sun looks dry, but increasing cloud and chances 
for rain are expected thru the day. That moisture from Isaias 
will be pushing north but will meet pretty strong resistance 
from the building high pressure branching across the Great Lakes
from central Canada. Rain will be most likely from the White 
Mtns to Penobscot Bay southward, and here NBM PoP looks pretty 
good. The QPF is a lower confidence forecast. Right now ensemble
guidance is pretty bearish on significant rainfall. The 
probabilities for at least a half inch of rain are generally 
around 1 in 3 for southernmost NH, and this is driven primarily 
because of the GEPS with some support from the deterministic 
NAM. The probabilities for a wetting rain (at least a tenth of 
an inch) are at least 60 percent from a LEB to PWM line south to
the Mass border. So this is looking like a fairly run of the 
mill high PoP/lower QPF event. The only unfortunate thing is 
that much of the rain will fall outside of the areas that need 
it the most. A frontal boundary will remain draped across the
forecast area thru Mon and may provide a focus for some isolated
showers during the day, but otherwise should hold off until the
next shortwave arrives.

Some showers are possible Monday night as a front sags 
southward into the area, mainly in the mountains. Behind this 
front, high pressure builds in to our north with northeast winds
bringing colder air into the region. This colder air may play a
role on Tuesday but is uncertain and more on that below.

Overall, Tuesday is looking like a wet day. A wave of low 
pressure will ride along the boundary and allow mostly rain to 
overspread the area from west to east in the morning and 
afternoon that will likely stick around through Tuesday night. I
say mostly rain as there indications of CAD for at least some 
of the day as the high shifts off to the north and east, which 
would keep temperatures colder for longer and could result in 
some wintry precipitation across the north, especially if the 
track of the low trends farther south (like the NAM solution and
to some extent the CMC). If to occur, the better chances would 
be in the western ME mountains with the NAM suggesting as far 
south as the foothills. However, the NAM is the outlier at this 
point when compared with much of the ensemble guidance from 
global models.

Back to rainfall amounts: Ensemble means from the GFS/ECWMF are
in pretty good agreement with rainfall amounts of 0.50" to 
1.00" of rain possible for much of the area through Wednesday 
morning, except less amounts of 0.25" to 0.50" toward parts of 
central and southern NH. 

Models are in a little better agreement than this time 
yesterday in regards to the timing of the cold front passing and
the widespread precipitation winding down...generally sometime 
Wednesday morning. Behind the front, west to northwest winds 
will become breezy with guidance suggesting 25-35 mph possible 
during the day Wednesday, but additional showers will be 
possible as a 500mb shortwave swings through. Higher chances 
will be in the mountains through Wednesday night with upslope 
flow, where colder air moving in could also change these over to
snow showers.

Thursday looks to remain breezy with good mixing and a tight 
gradient between low pressure in the Canadian Maritimes and high
pressure building from the west. Upslope rain/snow showers may 
continue in the the mountains into the first part of the day, 
but elsewhere should remain precip-free as the airmass looks 
drier. Rain chances increase again Friday and Saturday as the 
next front approaches.
